investigate:magnets.summary:
MAGNETS LENS. Short answer to the owner: no, mounting magnets does not steer radio waves or their field lines in air, and it has real costs. Magnetism does matter inside specific materials (ferrites, YIG, plasma), but none of the magnetic components is worth adding to rev B. The useful outputs are three design rules and two observing ideas.

1. Why static magnets do nothing in air. Maxwell's equations in vacuum, air, copper and FR-4 are linear with field-independent eps, mu, sigma. A static solution (E0,B0) and an RF solution (E1,B1) therefore add: the total is a solution and neither appears in the other's equations. The cross term in energy density, B0.B1/mu0, time-averages to zero, and the Poynting cross term carries no net power. Vacuum only turns nonlinear near the Schwinger field, 4.4e9 T. In copper the static-field (Hall) term is omega_c*tau = 4.4e-3 at 1 T and 4e-5 at 10 mT (my estimate, tau = 2.5e-14 s). So the "field lines" of a magnet and of a wave simply coexist. The Sun differs because its medium is a conducting plasma, where field and matter are coupled; air is not.

2. What a nearby magnet actually does (all derived estimates). Sintered NdFeB is a metal (110-170 micro-ohm cm): skin depth 21/13/8 um at 0.9/2.4/5.8 GHz, so a 10 mm magnet is a nickel-plated scatterer, lambda/5 at 5.8 GHz inside a 25 mm cell. A 10 mm N42 cube (moment 1.03 A m^2) gives 207 uT on axis at 10 cm, 7.7 uT at 30 cm, 1.7 uT at 50 cm, 0.2 uT at 1 m: against a ~20 uT horizontal Earth field that is up to 22 deg heading error at 30 cm, 4.7 deg at 50 cm, 0.6 deg at 1 m unless it is rigidly fixed to the sensor and calibrated out as hard iron. Gimbal motors and any circulator or YIG magnet do the same. Magnets also saturate ferrite-cored parts already on the board (TCM1-83X+ baluns, beads, chokes).

3. Where magnetism matters. In a magnetised ferrite the Polder tensor has chi_xx = w0*wm/(w0^2-w^2) and chi_xy = j*w*wm/(w0^2-w^2), with gamma = 28 GHz/T; the two circular polarisations see different mu, which gives Faraday rotation, circulators, isolators, ferrite phase shifters and YIG resonators. YIG spheres resonate at f = 28 GHz/T * B (82 mT at 2.3 GHz, 214 mT at 6 GHz); pure YIG cannot go below gamma*Ms/3 = 1.66 GHz.

4. Verdicts for array16.
- Circulator in the radar path: NO. New SMA units give about 20 dB isolation (800-960 MHz $439; 2-4 GHz $756-1,133; 2-6 GHz only 14 dB at $1,450), and antenna return loss of 10-15 dB caps monostatic leakage at -10 to -15 dB anyway. Rev B's separate horn gives >=60 dB and its own budget says isolation dominates range. SMT narrowband parts are cheap ($9-14 at 2.3-2.4 GHz) but solve nothing here.
- YIG preselector: NO. A 2-8 GHz unit has 5-7 dB loss, 30-50 MHz bandwidth, 20 MHz/mA, 10 MHz hysteresis, 15 MHz drift, 24 V heater at 0.1 A (2.4 W) plus 0.5 W coil at 6 GHz; four would be ~12 W against a 7.3 W board, cannot cover 0.4-1.7 GHz, cost $360-480 each surplus, and their ~40 ns group delay turns 1 MHz of mistracking into ~15 deg of inter-channel phase (150 deg across the hysteresis). The switched B1-B5 bank is better for a coherent array.
- Ferrite phase shifters: NO. They suit >100 W per element; they give phase, not true time delay, and do not fit a 25 mm cell.
- Magneto-dielectric substrates: NO. MAGTREX 555 (mu 6, eps 6.5) is low-loss only below 500 MHz; DF accuracy needs aperture, not smaller elements.
- Ionospheric Faraday rotation: real but benign. With 40 uT along the path: 17-339 deg at 400 MHz (5-100 TECU), 3-54 deg at 1 GHz, 1.3-27 deg at 1420 MHz. It is common to all elements, so bearings are unaffected; only amplitude fades. The HI line is unpolarised, so no effect.

5. Genuinely useful. (a) Keep all magnets, motors and steel >=0.5 m from the magnetometer or rigidly co-mounted and calibrated. (b) Faraday fading on 400-437 MHz linearly polarised satellite beacons is a free ionosphere (TEC) experiment with the whips. (c) Solar gyroresonance at 2.3-6 GHz maps to 270-1,070 G coronal fields, but reading it needs circular polarisation, which is an argument for a future dual-polarised tile.

findings.topic: Static magnets and RF in air
findings.claim: No steering. Maxwell's equations with field-independent eps, mu, sigma are linear, so a static field and an RF field superpose without interaction; cross terms in energy and Poynting flux average to zero. Vacuum nonlinearity only appears near the Schwinger limit (B about 4.4e9 T, E about 1.3e18 V/m).
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwinger_limit ; derivation from linearity of Maxwell's equations

findings.topic: Static field in ordinary antenna materials
findings.claim: In copper the magnetic (Hall) correction to conductivity is omega_c*tau = 4.4e-3 at 1 T, 8.8e-4 at 0.2 T, 4.4e-5 at 10 mT, so a magnet does not change how copper or FR-4 handle RF.
findings.source: estimate: omega_c = eB/m with copper tau = 2.5e-14 s; /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ascalva--claude-spares-spare-iFcbz1/8b6bf486-3081-448c-8f46-b00ba3ebceb0/scratchpad/fields/magnets.py

findings.topic: NdFeB magnet as an RF object
findings.claim: Sintered NdFeB has resistivity 110-170 micro-ohm cm, giving skin depth 20.5/12.6/8.1 um at 0.9/2.4/5.8 GHz (for 150 micro-ohm cm). It behaves as a metal scatterer that detunes nearby elements; a 10 mm magnet is about lambda/5 at 5.8 GHz.

Hard ferrite magnets are insulating, high-permittivity ceramic; they act as a lossy dielectric block near an element rather than a conductor. I did not find a sourced permittivity or loss figure at 0.4-6 GHz.
findings.source: estimate: general ferrite properties, no datasheet value retrieved

findings.claim: A 10 mm N42 cube (moment 1.03 A m^2) produces on-axis 207 uT at 10 cm, 25.9 uT at 20 cm, 7.7 uT at 30 cm, 1.7 uT at 50 cm, 0.21 uT at 1 m. Against a ~20 uT horizontal Earth field the worst-case uncalibrated heading error is 22.5 deg at 30 cm, 4.7 deg at 50 cm, 0.6 deg at 1 m.
findings.source: estimate: dipole field B = mu0*m/(2*pi*r^3), Br = 1.3 T; magnets.py

findings.claim: A magnet fixed in the sensor's frame adds a constant offset that calibration removes; sources that move relative to the sensor (motors, servos, high-current wiring, gimbal parts) cannot be fully compensated, and vendors advise mounting the sensor as far from them as possible.

For a ferrite biased along z, chi_xx = w0*wm/(w0^2-w^2) and chi_xy = j*w*wm/(w0^2-w^2) with w0 = gamma*mu0*H0, wm = gamma*mu0*Ms, gamma/2pi = 28.0 GHz/T. YIG (4piMs 1780 G) has fm = 4.98 GHz; a sphere resonates at 28 GHz/T times the bias (82 mT at 2.3 GHz, 214 mT at 6 GHz) and cannot be saturated below gamma*Ms/3 = 1.66 GHz.
findings.source: derivation (Landau-Lifshitz linearised) in magnets.py; lower limit agrees with ~1680 MHz stated in https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/4983936

findings.claim: Gallium substitution lowers magnetisation and lets YIG devices work to about 500 MHz (one source 360 MHz) at the cost of linewidth and Q, so a single YIG filter cannot span 0.4-6 GHz.

Micro Lambda 2-8 GHz filters: 3 dB bandwidth 30-50 MHz, insertion loss 5-7 dB, tuning 20 MHz/mA, coil 5-6 ohm and 40-60 mH, linearity +/-8 MHz, hysteresis 10 MHz, temperature drift 15 MHz, heater 24 V at 100 mA steady (300-500 mA surge), limiting at about +10 dBm, 0 to 65 C.

Per filter: coil 0.08 W at 2.3 GHz, 0.54 W at 6 GHz, plus 2.4 W heater; four channels need about 12 W against rev B's 7.3 W total. Group delay of about 40 ns (4 poles, 30 MHz) converts 1 MHz of channel-to-channel mistracking into about 15 deg of phase and the 10 MHz hysteresis into about 150 deg, which defeats coherent four-channel operation without recalibration after every retune.
findings.source: estimate: I = f/(20 MHz/mA), P = I^2 * 6 ohm, tau = N/(pi*BW); magnets.py

findings.claim: Full-range tuning takes roughly 1-10 ms for standard YIG filters (0.1-1 ms for fast designs), with hysteresis needing a settling or de-hysteresis step; rev B's switch bank changes band inside a 15 us slot.
findings.source: https://rfessentials.com/rf-knowledge-base/how-do-i-design-a-yig-tunable-bandpass-filter-for-a-wideband-receiver/ (secondary, unsourced figures); REDESIGN.md section on firmware

findings.claim: Surplus asking prices seen: Agilent YIG filter $360 and $479, Microsource 2.7-22 GHz 300 GBP; YIG oscillators from about $50. I found no published new price; new units are quote-only (my estimate: low thousands of dollars each).
findings.source: https://www.ebay.com/str/ronenct1 ; https://www.ebay.de/itm/283632079069 ; https://www.ebay.com/itm/304875490110 ; estimate for new price

findings.claim: New SMA circulators: Fairview SFC8096 800-960 MHz, 19 dB, $439; DiTom D3C2040 2-4 GHz, 20 dB, 0.4 dB loss, $756; Pasternack PE83CR1004 2-4 GHz $1,133; Pasternack PE8432 2-6 GHz, only 14 dB isolation, 0.8 dB loss, $1,450. SMT narrowband: Molex 2.3-2.4 GHz 20 dB about $9-14; Skyworks SKYFR-001736 2.4-2.5 GHz 23 dB, 0.14-0.20 dB; SKYFR-001301 5.15-5.85 GHz 20 dB (last-time buy); M/A-COM MAFRIN0461 902-928 MHz 29 dB typical.

findings.topic: Circulator in the radar path: verdict
findings.claim: Not worth it. A single-antenna radar through a circulator leaks transmit power at about the antenna return loss (-10 to -15 dB) or the circulator isolation (14-23 dB), whichever is worse, versus the >=60 dB that rev B gets from a horn 1.5 m aside; REDESIGN.md section 7 states isolation and nulling matter more than power. One circulator also covers only one band.

findings.topic: Ferrite phase shifters versus semiconductor true-time delay
findings.claim: Not worth it. Ferrite shifters offer 0.3-1 dB loss and 100 W to 10 kW handling with 1-100 us switching and are preferred above about 100 W per element; below about 10 W per element diode or MMIC parts win on cost, speed and weight. They provide phase, not delay, so they would squint over 2.3-6 GHz where rev B's 4-bit delay lines (2.6 dB, switched in a 15 us slot) do not, and waveguide or toroid parts do not fit a 25 mm cell (my estimate).

Not worth it. Rogers MAGTREX 555 has mu about 6 and eps about 6.5 with low loss only below 500 MHz, claiming up to 6x size reduction; Y/Z-type hexaferrites have magnetic loss tangent above 0.5 beyond 0.5 GHz (Snoek's limit). Only the bottom of the 0.4-2.3 GHz whip band could benefit, and direction-finding accuracy is set by array aperture (ring radius 112-225 mm), not element size.
findings.source: https://www.rogerscorp.com/advanced-electronics-solutions/magtrex-555-high-impedance-laminates ; https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10947367 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0603116 ; REDESIGN.md section on external layouts

findings.claim: Omega = [e^3/(8 pi^2 eps0 m^2 c)] * B_par * TEC / f^2 = 2.365e4 * B*TEC/f^2 rad (SI). With B_par = 40 uT and TEC 5/20/50/100 TECU: 400 MHz 17/68/169/339 deg; 435 MHz 14/57/143/286 deg; 915 MHz 3/13/32/65 deg; 1 GHz 3/11/27/54 deg; 1420 MHz 1.3/5.4/13/27 deg; 2.3 GHz 0.5/2/5/10 deg. ITU-R P.531 gives 108 deg at 1 GHz as the estimated maximum at 30 deg elevation, scaling as 1/f^2.

findings.topic: Faraday rotation effect on DF and astronomy
findings.claim: The rotation is the same at every element, so it adds no inter-element phase error and does not bias bearings; it only changes amplitude by cos^2 of the mismatch (XPD = 20 log tan Omega), which can fade a linearly polarised satellite signal on a linear whip at 400-900 MHz. Across a 20 MHz capture at 400 MHz and 50 TECU the angle changes by about 17 deg. The 1420 MHz hydrogen line and quiet-Sun emission are unpolarised, so they are unaffected.

findings.topic: Solar magnetised plasma in the panel band
findings.claim: Gyroresonance emission above sunspots comes from the 2nd and 3rd harmonics of the electron gyrofrequency (2.8 MHz per gauss), so 2.3-6 GHz corresponds to coronal fields of 274-1,072 G, inside the 200-3,000 G range microwaves are sensitive to. The signature is strong circular polarisation whose sign follows the field direction, which a single linear polarisation cannot measure.

For a 100 sfu Sun, one polarisation, the antenna temperature rise is about 2.1 K for a 2.15 dBi whip at 1.42 GHz, 1.7 K for a 7 dBi panel beam at 2.8 GHz and 2.7 K for 15.5 dBi at 5.8 GHz: under 1 % of system temperature, so it needs correlation or beam switching rather than total power. Actual solar flux differs by frequency and activity.

open_questions: Where will the IMU/magnetometer sit relative to gimbal motors, encoders with magnets, and steel mounts? The 0.5 m / 1 m distances above assume a 10 mm NdFeB magnet; motor stray fields need the motor's own data or a measurement.
Do the ferrite-cored parts on the core board (TCM1-83X+ baluns, bias beads) shift measurably near a motor or magnet? Not sourced; a bench check with a magnet at 2-5 cm would settle it.
New YIG filter prices and the Micro Lambda size/weight figures were not retrievable (quote-only, PDFs unreadable); the 'low thousands' new price is my estimate.
The microwaves101 ferrite phase shifter page returned 404, so the ferrite-versus-MMIC thresholds rest on an informal FAQ and old patents.
Hard ferrite magnet permittivity and loss at 0.4-6 GHz were not sourced.
Is a dual-polarised (or circular) tile variant of interest? It is the only way to use solar gyroresonance or to measure Faraday rotation directly, and it is outside rev B's one-polarisation scope.
Which linearly polarised 400-437 MHz satellite beacons are usable for the Faraday-fading TEC experiment at the owner's location was not researched.

investigate:extremes.summary:
Wrote and ran /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/fields_study.py (11 s; no existing file touched). All numbers below are from idealised models (thin-dipole induced-EMF for whips, cos^1.5 uncoupled flares for the panel), not full-wave runs.

**Owner's two questions**
- **Sun:** it does rotate (about 25 days at the equator, about 35 at the poles), and that differential rotation is what winds its field. The analogy that holds is "currents make the field; change the currents and the field structure changes". An array's fields superpose linearly, so beams and nulls are exactly constructive and destructive interference.
- **Magnets:** no. A static field does not steer radio waves in air; the vacuum effect is about 5e-23 rad over 0.1 m at 1 T. Magnets matter only inside ferrites and plasmas (circulators, ferrite phase shifters, ionosphere, sunspots). On this build a 10 mm N42 cube puts about 207 µT at 0.1 m and 1.7 µT at 0.5 m on the magnetometer, roughly a 5° heading error at 0.5 m. The one useful magnet is inside a bought circulator or isolator.

**(a) Electronic polarisation rotation is the one addition worth making.**
- The V-only panel loses 3 dB on circular or unpolarised signals, 6 dB at 60° tilt, and everything at 90°.
- Two V and two H quadrant channels measure tilt to 2.0° median (5.2° at the 95th percentile) and ellipticity to 1.9° in one capture, with no polarisation loss. With 0.1 dB / 1° calibration this becomes 0.7°.
- If V and H flares share a combiner, the existing 4-bit delay states already give quadrature: axial ratio is at most 1.03 dB over 2.3-6 GHz (median 0.20 dB).
- A linear polarisation spun at 8 kHz is one line at ±8 kHz in each circular hand. With 0/180 switches only, the wanted line is -3.9 dB and the worst image -13.5 dB.
- Cost (my estimate): about $40-60 for crossed cards plus a V/H switch per element, against about $233 and 4.6 W for 16 more full cells.

**(b) Pseudo-Doppler is already inside rev B and is worse than what rev B does.** Commutating one receiver round a ring yields phase mode l = 1 taken in time. Its bias is 3.4-13.8° on rev B's 4-whip rings and it gives up 6-12 dB against simultaneous channels. Time-modulated tricks are limited by the 15 µs slot to signals of a few kHz (my estimate).

**(c) Vortex beams: no new capability; one free use.**
- A ring of N makes |l| < N/2, and purity collapses once k·a exceeds about N - |l|. The 225 mm ring of 8 is pure only up to about 0.9 GHz (l = 1 purity 18 % at 2.3 GHz); 16 on that ring stay pure to 2.3 GHz.
- Whips have a null on the ring axis, so their "vortex" is just circular-array phase modes.
- Ring-to-ring, the singular vectors are the OAM modes, and mode power falls as D^-2(|l|+1): l = 1 is -18 dB at 10 m and -38 dB at 100 m.
- The free use: l = 1 from the four panel quadrants is the monopulse difference pair (purity 99 % at 2.44 GHz, 85 % at 5.8 GHz), useful for tracking.

**(d) Superdirectivity: a modest win at 0.4 GHz, none worth having on the panel.**
- Two whips: 6.7 dBi at 0.25 λ (Q 12, 5.7 % bandwidth, 33 Ω), rising only to 7.4 dBi at 0.1 λ (Q 50, 1.4 %, 6.8 Ω).
- Four whips at 0.25 λ: 11.9 dBi lossless, 10.3 dBi with 2 Ω loss, 11.5 dBi with 3° / 0.5 dB errors, Q 141. At 0.1 λ it is 12.7 dBi on paper, but Q is 25,000 and gain falls to 4.4 dBi with those errors.
- On receive, a 0.25 λ pair beats a λ/2 pair by 1.3-1.9 dB only when external noise is 3-10 times receiver noise. Rev B's 4-whip rings already sit at 0.25-0.45 λ spacing.
- Panel at 2.44 GHz: 13.6 dBi against 10.6 dBi uniform, but at 10-13 dB lower white-noise gain; nothing to gain at 5.8 GHz.

**(e) Near field.** The reactive zone is 119 mm at 0.4 GHz and 8 mm at 6 GHz. The far field starts at 0.39 m for the panel at 5.8 GHz and 3.1 m for the plate at 2.3 GHz. Wavefront curvature across the plate exceeds 3° inside 23 m at 2.3 GHz, so indoor range is measurable and close calibration sources need the spherical correction. A passive 0.5 m flat plate at 10 m + 10 m, 5.8 GHz, returns about -0.3 dB relative to the direct path; a switchable surface is not worth building.

findings.claim: The Sun does rotate (about 25 days at the equator, about 35 at the poles); that differential rotation winds the field in about 8 months per wrap and drives the dynamo. The valid analogy for the array is that currents make the fields; unlike solar plasma, array fields superpose linearly, so beams and nulls are pure interference and move when phases or delays change.

Magnets do not steer radio waves in air or vacuum. Maxwell's equations are linear there; the QED vacuum birefringence is about 4e-24 per T^2, giving about 5e-23 rad over 0.1 m at 1 T and 6 GHz. The Schwinger field is 4.4e9 T.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.12913.pdf (PVLAS) ; derivation: phase = 2 pi L dn / lambda

findings.claim: Static fields matter only in gyrotropic media: ferrites (circulators, isolators, ferrite phase shifters that steered early phased arrays) and plasmas (electron gyrofrequency 28 GHz/T, so 1.4 MHz in Earth's 50 uT; Faraday rotation scales as lambda^2). For rev B the only useful magnet is inside a bought circulator or isolator on the radar or transmit path.

Magnets on the mount harm the planned magnetometer: a 10 mm N42 cube (Br 1.3 T, moment about 1.03 A m^2) gives about 207 uT at 0.1 m, 13 uT at 0.25 m and 1.7 uT at 0.5 m on axis, a heading error of about 5 deg at 0.5 m against a 20 uT horizontal field. A magnet fixed to the sensor body is a calibratable hard-iron offset; one that moves relative to it (gimbal, magnetic encoder) is not. Ferrite-cored parts could also be biased at close range.
findings.source: estimate: dipole field B = mu0 m / (2 pi r^3), Br 1.3 T from general knowledge; hard-iron behaviour https://mtidocs.xsens.com/magnetic-distortion-theory

findings.claim: Rev B already moves beams and nulls without motion: 4-bit true-time delays per flare, 0/180 polarity per channel, four coherent channels for digital beams and three nulls, and Latin-square port selection. What it cannot do is change polarisation: one linear polarisation loses 3 dB on circular or unpolarised signals, 6 dB at 60 deg tilt, 11.7 dB at 75 deg, and everything at 90 deg.

With two V and two H quadrant channels, one 64-sample capture at 20 dB per element gives tilt error 2.0 deg median / 5.2 deg at the 95th percentile and ellipticity error 1.9 / 5.1 deg, with median recovered power 0.0 dB. The error is set by the 0.5 dB / 3 deg residual and -20 dB cross-polar, not by SNR (0 dB SNR: 2.8 / 8.5 deg). With 0.1 dB / 1 deg and -30 dB cross-polar it is 0.7 / 2.0 deg.

Mechanical roll (rotation_study) needs at least 3 roll angles and reaches 0.3 deg only if source power is steady between captures; with 1 dB power change it degrades to 2.7-3.6 deg. Dual-pol measures in one capture and is immune to source fading.

If a V and an H flare feed the same combiner, the existing delay states (38.5/52.5/117.5/139 ps) already supply quadrature: best state pair is within 6.7 deg of 90 deg everywhere in 2.3-6 GHz, axial ratio at most 1.03 dB, median 0.20 dB. No new phase shifter is needed for analogue circular polarisation. The channel residual of 0.7 dB / 4.2 deg between two channels adds about 0.95 dB axial ratio (25 dB cross-hand rejection).
findings.source: /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/fields/tables.md tables 3b, 3c ; assumes state delay = sum of selected bits

findings.claim: A linear polarisation turned at f_rot with weights (cos, sin) on V and H is exactly one line at +f_rot in one circular hand and -f_rot in the other, each -3.0 dB. With only 0/180 switches (four states per turn) the wanted line is -3.9 dB and the strongest images are -13.5 dB (3rd) and -17.9 dB (5th).

Cheapest route for the panel: crossed (egg-crate) cards plus one V/H select switch per element ahead of the LNA, about $40-60 extra, 16 more control bits and 0.15-0.6 dB more noise figure. Full dual chains cost about $233 more and about 4.6 W, which breaks the 5 V / 3 A budget. Egg-crate Vivaldi arrays are standard but have high diagonal-plane cross-polar and are sensitive to unused-port terminations, so the openEMS model must be redone. Whips are V-only; dual-pol below 2.3 GHz means separate crossed dipoles or turnstiles.
findings.source: estimate: from REDESIGN.md section 10 costs (cells $233 for 16, BGS12WN6 $0.32, 58 mA per LNA) ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.11020

findings.claim: Commutating one receiver round a ring gives, in its first harmonic, exactly phase mode l = 1 of the ring (N j J1(kr) e^{j phi0} plus aliases J_(N-1)). Worst bearing bias before lookup correction: 3.4 / 7.2 / 13.8 deg for 4 whips at r = 0.18 / 0.25 / 0.32 wavelengths (rev B's rings), 8.2 deg for 8 whips on 225 mm at 0.915 GHz, unusable at 2.3 GHz. It also costs 6 / 9 / 12 dB of SNR against 4 / 8 / 16 simultaneous elements. Rev B's coherent time-multiplexed sampling gets the same information without these losses.

Rev B's 15 us minimum slot lets a ring of 4 / 8 / 16 be commutated at up to 16.7 / 8.3 / 4.2 kHz. The HackRF-only mode with 0/180 Hadamard coding is already a time-modulated array. Harmonic beam steering and sideband frequency translation are possible in principle but only for signals narrower than a few kHz, and sidebands waste power. Space-time-modulated non-reciprocity is real but needs modulation faster than the signal bandwidth; a ferrite circulator or the separate radar horn is the practical route.
findings.source: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/17/3/590/html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4822645 ; estimate for the bandwidth limit from REDESIGN.md section 8 slot time

findings.claim: A ring of N elements makes modes |l| < N/2; |l| = N/2 is a standing pattern (50 % purity). Purity over the half space collapses once k a exceeds about N - |l|. For N = 8: l = 1..3 are 100 % pure at k a = 2, 100/99/94 % at k a = 4, 51/44/50 % at k a = 8. For N = 16: all of l = 1..6 are at least 99 % at k a = 8.
findings.source: /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/fields/tables.md table 1a ; derivation: AF = N sum_q j^(l+qN) J_(l+qN)(k a sin theta) e^{j(l+qN) phi}

findings.claim: The 225 mm ring of 8 (k a = 1.89 / 4.31 / 6.70 / 10.85 at 0.4 / 0.915 / 1.42 / 2.3 GHz) gives pure vortices only up to about 0.9 GHz: l = 1 half-space purity for transverse elements is 100 / 100 / 81 / 29 %. Sixteen elements on that ring stay at 98-100 % to 2.3 GHz. The vortex cone half-angle for l = 1 narrows from 25 deg at 0.915 GHz to 10 deg at 2.3 GHz, and peak directivity is 2-6 dB below the same ring fed in phase. Whips have a null on the ring axis, so their vortex is really the circular-array phase modes seen at the horizon.

For two facing rings of 8 at 225 mm, 2.3 GHz (Rayleigh distance 3.1 m), the channel matrix is circulant, so its singular vectors are the OAM modes: OAM multiplexing is ordinary MIMO. Mode power relative to l = 0 is -8.6 / -22.3 dB (l = 1 / 2) at 3 m, -18.3 / -42.6 dB at 10 m, -38.3 / -82.6 dB at 100 m; fitted far-field slopes are D^-2, -4, -6, -8, -10 for l = 0..4. No capacity beyond MIMO in the far field.

The l = 1 mode formed from the four panel quadrants is exactly the monopulse difference pair (A - C) + j(B - D): on-axis null, phase equal to the azimuth of the pointing error. Purity is 99 / 96 / 85 % at 2.44 / 3.5 / 5.8 GHz with cone half-angles 39 / 32 / 20 deg. It costs no hardware and gives a two-axis tracking error signal for a gimbal following the Sun or a satellite. l = 2 from four quadrants is not a vortex (50 % purity).

Two whips end-fire (dipole model; add 3 dB over ideal ground): 6.7 dBi at 0.25 wavelength (R_eff 33 ohm, Q 12, 5.7 % bandwidth), 7.4 dBi at 0.1 wavelength (6.8 ohm, Q 50, 1.4 %, 77 % efficient with 2 ohm loss), limit 7.5 dBi. Ordinary end-fire at lambda/2 is 4.4 dBi. Model check: half-wave Z11 = 73.1 + 42.5j, Z12 at lambda/2 = -12.5 - 29.9j, both textbook values; the 7.5 dBi limit agrees with the roughly 7 dB reported for two-element supergain arrays.

Three and four elements are only practical near 0.25 wavelength. N = 4 at 0.25: 11.9 dBi lossless, R_eff 3.0 ohm, Q 141 (0.5 % bandwidth), 10.3 dBi with 2 ohm loss, 11.5 dBi mean with 3 deg / 0.5 dB errors. N = 4 at 0.1: 12.7 dBi on paper, R_eff 0.01 ohm, Q about 25,000, 8.2 dBi with 2 ohm loss and 4.4 dBi with 3 deg errors. N = 3 at 0.1: 10.4 dBi, Q 989, 8.2 dBi with errors.

With an LNA per whip, the SNR gain is 10 log N whenever receiver noise dominates, whatever the spacing. Close spacing helps only when external noise dominates: for external/receiver noise ratio 3-10, a 0.25 wavelength pair gives 3.8-4.3 dB against 2.4-2.5 dB at lambda/2, and four whips 6.5-7.3 dB against 4.9-5.1 dB. Below 0.15 wavelength it gets worse again. Rev B's 4-whip rings (r/lambda 0.18-0.32, adjacent spacing 0.25-0.45 wavelength) are already near this optimum.
findings.source: /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/fields/tables.md table 2b ; noise ratio at 0.4 GHz is an estimate extrapolated from ITU-R P.372 (valid to 250 MHz) https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/p/R-REC-P.372-15-202109-I!!PDF-E.pdf

findings.claim: Idealised (no coupling): at 2.44 GHz broadside uniform weights give 10.6 dBi (above the 9.2 dBi 4 pi A / lambda^2 figure because a 0.8-wavelength aperture collects beyond its edges); optimum weights give 13.6 dBi but at -13 dB white-noise gain (-9.9 dB for the error-robust design). At 3.5 GHz the gain is +1.2 dB for -3 dB; at 5.8 GHz there is nothing (17.0 dBi either way). Since the panel is receiver-noise limited, this trades 3 dB of directivity for about 10 dB of SNR: useful only as a narrower beam against interference.

Harrington normal gain (ka)^2 + 2ka: 7.2 dBi for one whip plus image (ka 1.49), 8.6 dBi for the 133 mm 4-whip ring (ka 1.86), 10.3 dBi for the whole plate at 0.4 GHz (ka 2.43), 12.7 dBi for the active panel at 2.3 GHz (ka 3.41), 19.6 dBi at 5.8 GHz. Chu Q bound 1/(ka)^3 + 1/ka is below 1 for all of them, so the Q penalty comes from the superdirective current set, not from element size.

Reactive zone lambda/2pi: 119 mm at 0.4 GHz, 20 mm at 2.44 GHz, 8 mm at 6 GHz, so whips on the plate and neighbouring flares sit in each other's reactive fields (hence the mandatory measured manifold). Far field 2D^2/lambda: 0.16 m (panel, 2.44 GHz), 0.39 m (panel, 5.8 GHz), 0.54 m (plate, 0.4 GHz), 3.1 m (plate, 2.3 GHz). Wavefront curvature at the plate rim exceeds 3 deg inside 9 m at 0.915 GHz and 23 m at 2.3 GHz, so indoor source range is measurable and manifold sources at 5 m need the spherical-phase correction rev B already plans.
findings.source: estimate: derivation k a^2 / (2R) with a = 225 mm ; REDESIGN.md section 4

findings.claim: A passive reflecting surface obeys a product-distance law, received power proportional to A^2 / (d1 d2)^2. A 0.5 m square flat plate at 10 m + 10 m and 5.8 GHz returns about -0.3 dB relative to the direct 20 m path, but only at its specular angle. A plain plate or corner reflector is a useful radar and calibration target; a reconfigurable surface needs hundreds of switched cells (the measured ones had 256 to 10,200) and is not worth building for this project.
findings.source: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05326 (Tang et al., eq. 6) ; plate figure is an estimate from that formula

findings.claim: Dual polarisation is the field-related upgrade with a science use: sunspot gyroresonance emission is circularly polarised and its frequency maps to field strength (third harmonic at 6 cm corresponds to about 550-600 G), and professional solar polarimeters record Stokes I and V at 1, 2, 3.75 and 9.4 GHz. The quiet Sun would add only about 1.4 K at 2.44 GHz and 4 K at 5.8 GHz to the bare panel, so it needs a dish or interferometric correlation between quadrants.
findings.source: https://solar.nro.nao.ac.jp/norp/html/introduction.html ; https://www.astro.umd.edu/~white/papers/02_potsdam.pdf ; antenna temperatures are estimates from REDESIGN gains with assumed 75 and 150 sfu

open_questions: Dual-pol panel: is a V/H select switch per element (two quadrants V, two H at once) acceptable, or is simultaneous dual-pol on all 16 elements wanted? The latter needs about $233 and 4.6 W more and breaks the 5 V / 3 A budget.

An egg-crate (crossed-card) connected Vivaldi has not been simulated: cross-polar level, diagonal-plane behaviour and the effect of 36 card crossings on the 2.3-3 GHz match need the openEMS model before committing.

The delay-line quadrature result (axial ratio at most 1.03 dB) assumes each delay state is the plain sum of its bits and ignores line dispersion and loss imbalance; it should be rechecked against the measured delay tables.

The superdirective whip numbers use a thin-dipole induced-EMF model in free space; the finite 500 mm plate, 50 ohm LNA loading and noise coupling between LNAs are not modelled. A two-whip 0.25-wavelength test on the bench would settle the 1.3-1.9 dB receive gain.

The external-to-receiver noise ratio at 0.4 GHz (taken as 1-10) is extrapolated beyond the ITU-R P.372 model's 250 MHz limit; a measured noise floor at the owner's site would decide whether close whip spacing pays at all.
Quiet-Sun flux at 5.8 GHz (150 sfu) and the resulting 4 K antenna temperature are my estimates; receiver_study.md should own the radio-astronomy sensitivity figures.
If rotation_study selects magnetic encoders, their magnets and the IMU magnetometer need a stated separation or the encoders should be optical; I did not see that study's final choice.
No experiments/fields_study.md was written (the task named only the script and its outputs); the generated tables are in experiments/fields/tables.md.

investigate:sun.summary:
Lens: the Sun, as the owner's analogy and as a target. The web-search quota (shared by all agents) was already used up, so I fetched every source directly from a known URL, or read it from paper texts that an earlier run of this lens had saved in scratch. Numbers come from public data downloaded today (2026-11-15), run through sun_study.py. No repository files were changed.

The analogy, answered honestly. The Sun does rotate, but not as a solid body: about 25 days at the equator, 33-38 days near the poles, 27.3 days as seen from Earth. That shear drives the dynamo:
- differential rotation winds the north-south (poloidal) field into a strong east-west (toroidal) field;
- that field rises by buoyancy and breaks the surface as pairs of sunspots of opposite polarity, and the polarity flips every 11 years (a 22-year magnetic cycle);
- the field is frozen into the conducting plasma until opposite fields are squeezed into thin current sheets, where reconnection turns magnetic energy into heat and fast particles (flares, coronal mass ejections).

That "construct and destruct" needs a nonlinear plasma. array16's fields are in vacuum, where they simply add. Changing element currents reshapes interference patterns without moving anything, but nothing can reconnect. You can even watch the rotation: F10.7 (the 2800 MHz solar flux index) went from 89 to 137 sfu in two weeks this month. In active years its 27-day swing is 45-51 %; at solar minimum it is 6-7 %.

Magnets: no, they would not steer anything. A static field changes radio waves only through free electrons or magnetic materials. In the corona the electron gyrofrequency (2.80 MHz per gauss) reaches GHz over sunspots, which makes the plasma emit, split waves into two modes, and circularly polarise solar radio emission. Near the array there is no such medium:
- in air the electron plasma frequency stays below 1 MHz, even at 10^4 electrons/cm³;
- in copper the Hall angle is 4.4e-3 rad at 1 T;
- in vacuum the induced birefringence is about 3e-24 at 1 T.

A magnet would harm the planned magnetometer. A 25 mm N52 cube gives 3.8 mT at 10 cm, beyond the ±16 G range of a LIS3MDL, and still about one Earth field at 0.5 m.

The Sun as a target. Learmonth quiet-Sun flux from the deep minimum (Oct 2019) to the maximum (Jul-Aug 2024): 410 MHz 26→49, 610 MHz 33→79, 1415 MHz 44→142, 2695 MHz 61→193, 4995 MHz 104→199 sfu. The activity component therefore peaks near 2.7 GHz. DRAO F10.7 noon values for 2004-2026 range from 64.0 sfu at minimum to a 2024 median of 183 and burst-contaminated values up to 939; today it is 122. Over the last 31 days, RSTN reported 7 distinct bursts of at least 100 sfu between 410 and 4995 MHz; the largest was 430 sfu at 2695 MHz.

What array16 can see:
- **Panel at 2695 MHz** (16 elements, four channels summed): the quiet Sun now adds 2.3 K in one polarisation against a system temperature of 320-470 K. That is a 0.02-0.03 dB rise; DRAO's 1.8 m dish sees about 5 dB. The statistics are easy (switched SNR 8-11 in 1 s), but a plain total-power measurement needs gain held to 7e-4.
- **Two-element interferometer:** the panel correlated with a 13 dBi grid (or a whip) on an external port 1-2 m away gives SNR about 70 per second. The fringe period is 13-25 min, ground and sky emission are resolved out, and flux is good to about 0.2 % per minute (statistics only).
- **Whips at 408 MHz** are the best burst detectors: the Sun is 4.8 % of system temperature, and a 3 sfu burst is a 5σ event in 1 s.
- **Large bursts:** they never overload the receivers. A 10^6 sfu event costs GNSS receivers 21-25 dB of C/N0.

Useful for the project:
- **Frequencies:** observe in the protected 2690-2700 MHz band (RSTN's 2695 MHz) rather than at 2800 MHz, which sits in a radar band right above the 2500-2690 MHz mobile bands.
- **Daily calibration:** compare each day with the machine-readable DRAO, RSTN and IPS values. The reference stations themselves disagree by a median of 8-16 %.
- **Manifold calibration:** the Sun is a free far-field source inside the restricted bands where rev B may not radiate its own calibration signal. Estimate: about 0.5-0.7° per element per minute.
- **Heading for moving mounts:** the Sun's direction plus gravity gives full attitude (the TRIAD method) to about 0.1-0.2°. A magnetometer can be off by 0.3-3° during a geomagnetic storm.

Dual polarisation. Solar emission has essentially no linear polarisation, so the single-polarisation panel measures half the total flux without bias. However, it can never measure circular polarisation (Stokes V), however it is rolled. Two orthogonal linear feeds, cross-correlated, give V. Whole-disk V is usually a few % because the two hemispheres cancel; flares reach tens of %. Feeds with -20 dB cross-polarisation therefore need their leakage calibrated, to about 2 %.

Hobby context: e-CALLISTO (at least 150 stations, 45-870 MHz), Radio JOVE, SuperSID (over 2,500 monitors), the Haystack SRT, and HamSCI magnetometers. array16 would extend amateur coverage to 0.87-6 GHz and add a direction check for rejecting interference.

findings.topic: Owner's premise: is the Sun rotating?
findings.claim: Yes, and not as a solid body. The equatorial sidereal period is about 24.5-25.7 days (the article gives both values), 33.4 days at 75° latitude, and almost 38 days synodic near the poles. The Carrington synodic period is 27.2753 days. Surface rate: omega = 14.713 - 2.396 sin^2(lat) - 1.787 sin^4(lat) deg/day. Inside, the convection zone rotates differentially, and below the tachocline the radiative zone turns almost as a solid body.

findings.topic: How the Sun's field is built and flipped (dynamo)
findings.claim: Differential rotation in the tachocline winds the weak poloidal field into a much stronger toroidal field. Buoyant upwelling makes that field emerge as east-west pairs of opposite-polarity sunspots. The pairs' polarity alternates each cycle (Hale cycle), and the 22-year Babcock-Leighton cycle covers two reversals of the polar dipole.

findings.topic: Construct and destruct: frozen-in flux and reconnection, and the antenna contrast
findings.claim: At large magnetic Reynolds number, the field and the plasma move together (Alfvén's theorem). The approximation breaks down in current sheets, where reconnection rearranges field topology and turns magnetic energy into kinetic energy (flares, CMEs). In vacuum the field equations are linear, so array16 can only superpose and steer interference patterns. Nothing can reconnect or release stored field energy; the only stored energy is reactive near-field energy, whose cost the fields study already quantified (superdirectivity).

findings.topic: Solar radio emission mechanisms and polarisation
findings.claim: Free-free emission dominates the quiet Sun. Gyroresonance comes mainly from the 2nd and 3rd gyro-harmonics over sunspots; x-mode opacity is about 10 times o-mode, so polarisation can approach 100 % and its sense follows spot polarity. Gyrosynchrotron is the main flare mechanism above 1-2 GHz (x-mode where optically thin, o-mode where thick). Linear polarisation is hard to detect because coronal Faraday rotation is large.

findings.topic: Which coronal layer array16 sees at each frequency (derived)
findings.claim: The gyrofrequency is 2.7992 MHz per gauss (27.99 GHz per tesla). At 2695 MHz, gyroresonance comes from the layer where |B| = 481 G (s=2) or 321 G (s=3); at 4995 MHz from 892 or 595 G; at 1420 MHz from 254 or 169 G. Plasma emission at 2695 MHz needs n_e = 9.0e10 cm^-3 (2.25e10 for the second harmonic), which only dense flare loops have. At 408 MHz it needs 2.1e9 (5.2e8). In effect, the array's frequency selects a coronal field strength.
findings.source: derivation: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ascalva--claude-spares-spare-iFcbz1/8b6bf486-3081-448c-8f46-b00ba3ebceb0/scratchpad/fields/sun/sun_tables.txt table G1 (f_B = eB/2 pi m_e, f_p = 8.98 kHz sqrt(n_e))

findings.claim: Type I: noise storms at about 50-500 MHz, high circular polarisation. Type II: slow drift (~0.05 MHz/s) from CME shocks near 1000 km/s, little polarisation. Type III: fast drift (~100 MHz/s) from electron beams at 0.1-0.3c, usually below 50 % circular. Type IV: broadband continuum (moving types with CMEs; storm continuum more strongly polarised). Type V: follows type III below about 120 MHz. SWPC alerts show one type II (estimated 1972 km/s) and one type IV on 2026-11-14 at about 21:30 UT.

findings.topic: What F10.7 is and how DRAO measures it
findings.claim: F10.7 is the solar flux in a 100 MHz band centred on 2800 MHz, averaged over an hour, measured three times a day (17/20/23 UT; 18/20/22 UT in winter). It uses two 1.8 m dishes on equatorial mounts at DRAO Penticton, calibrated against a reference horn to about 1 %; measurements have run since 1947, and 1 sfu = 1e-22 W m^-2 Hz^-1. It is the quiet-Sun free-free emission plus the slowly varying component (free-free over plage and gyroresonance over spots, with a broad spectral peak near 10 cm), plus any bursts. The beam must taper by no more than about 1 % across the disk.

8,044 DRAO noon values from 2004-10-28 to 2026-11-15: minimum 64.0 sfu (2019-10-21). The solar-minimum years have a median of 69-70 and a 1st percentile near 65. The 2024 maximum year has a median of 182.5 and a 99th percentile of 304. Burst-contaminated noon values reach 401-939 sfu (for example 573.4 on 2006-12-06). Observed/adjusted ranges 0.966-1.035 (Earth-Sun distance). The cycle-25 smoothed peak was October 2024 (sunspot number 160.9, F10.7 194.5). SWPC says F10.7 varies 'from below 50 to above 300 sfu' over a cycle.

findings.topic: The Sun's rotation, visible in radio now
findings.claim: On 2026-11-15, F10.7 was 122 sfu at noon, with a 90-day mean of 112. Over the past 46 days it ran 92→137→89→132 sfu as active regions rotated onto and off the disk. The 27-day (max-min)/mean is 0.45 in 2026 and 0.51 in 2024, but only 0.06-0.07 at minimum. Day-to-day changes have a median of 1.8 % and a 95th percentile of 9 %. array16 needs day-to-day stability of a few % to see this rotation.

findings.topic: Solar spectrum across array16's band (same station)
findings.claim: Learmonth quiet-Sun values, deep minimum (21-25 Oct 2019) to maximum (Jul-Aug 2024): 410 MHz 26→48.5, 610 MHz 33→79, 1415 MHz 43.5→142, 2695 MHz 61→192.5, 4995 MHz 104→199, 8800 MHz 236→311, 15400 MHz 545→576 sfu. The activity component (max minus min) peaks at 2695 MHz (132 sfu), and the max/min ratio is largest at 1.4-2.7 GHz (3.2-3.3 times), which is the panel and upper-whip range. Disk-averaged brightness temperature at minimum over the optical disk: 7.4e5 K at 410 MHz, 1.0e5 K at 1415 MHz, 4.0e4 K at 2695 MHz.

findings.topic: How accurate the professional references are
findings.claim: Over the last 30 days, the four RSTN stations (Learmonth, San Vito, Sagamore Hill, Kaena Point) disagreed on the same day by a median of 8 % at 410 MHz, 16 % at 1415 MHz, 9 % at 2695 MHz and 15 % at 4995 MHz, with up to 18-32 % at worst. Calibrating against RSTN is therefore limited to about ±10 %, while DRAO F10.7 (about 1 %) is the standard at 2.8 GHz. IPS also publishes interpolated daily quiet-Sun values at 1300, 1540, 1707, 2300, 2401, 2790, 5625 and 6000 MHz.

findings.topic: How many bursts array16 would see
findings.claim: In the 31 days to 2026-11-15, RSTN reported 7 distinct bursts of at least 100 sfu between 410 and 4995 MHz, worldwide and around the clock. The largest were 430 sfu at 2695 MHz (2026-10-19, 1 min, with an M1.6 flare) and 690 sfu at 410 MHz (2026-10-24). The same month had 19 M-class and no X-class flares, plus 64 type III, 3 type II and 1 type IV bursts at 25-180 MHz. A single site observing about 8 hours a day would see roughly a third of these, about 2-3 per month (estimate).

47 CFR 2.106 protects 406.1-410 MHz (US74) and 608-614 MHz, and bars transmitters (US246) at 1400-1427, 1660.5-1668.4, 2690-2700 and 4990-5000 MHz; 1400-1427 and 2690-2700 MHz are also all-emissions-prohibited (5.340). RSTN's 410, 610, 1415, 2695 and 4995 MHz all fall inside these bands. F10.7's 2800 MHz sits in the 2700-2900 MHz radar band (5.337, 5.423), with mobile-broadband bands at 2500-2690 MHz just below (5.384A). array16 should therefore observe in 2690-2700 MHz with 10 MHz or less of bandwidth, not at 2800 MHz.

findings.topic: The panel against the quiet Sun at 2.7-2.8 GHz
findings.claim: Panel, 16 elements with the four channels summed in software, broadside, one polarisation. At 2695 MHz the effective area is 56.5 cm² (efficiency 0.56). The quiet Sun adds 1.25 K at the 2019 minimum, 2.33 K now (114 sfu) and 3.94 K at the 2024 maximum, against a system temperature of 324 K (pointed at the sky) or 465 K (antenna at 290 K). That is 0.5-0.7 %, or a 0.02-0.03 dB rise when pointed at the Sun; DRAO's 1.8 m dish sees about 5.4 dB. A switched receiver gives SNR 8-11 in 1 s at 10 MHz (1 % in about 80 s, statistically), but an unswitched measurement needs gain held to 7e-4 for 10 %. Bursts are seen at 5σ in 1 s from about 50-115 sfu. Single elements see only 0.15 K and quadrants 0.58 K.
findings.source: sun_tables.txt B and B2 (REDESIGN.md section 4 gains and section 5 noise figures; T_A = A_e S / 2k and Dicke sigma from https://www.cv.nrao.edu/~sransom/web/Ch3.html); system temperatures are estimates

findings.topic: Whips are the most sensitive solar total-power detectors
findings.claim: A 2 dBi whip at 408 MHz has an effective area of 681 cm². The Sun adds 6.9 K now against a 142 K system temperature (4.8 %), and a 3 sfu burst is a 5σ event in 1 s. At 1420 MHz the Sun adds 1.5 K (1 %). Four whips phased together give up to 4 times as much only if spaced at least half a wavelength apart; on the plate at 408 MHz the Harrington bound limits a 133 mm ring to about 2.3 times one whip.
findings.source: sun_tables.txt B (estimate: 2 dBi toward the Sun and 60-150 K antenna temperature, as in experiments/count/extras.txt and topology_study.py)

findings.claim: Gain fluctuations add T_sys·ΔG/G to a total-power receiver. Dicke switching reduces that to (T1-T2)·ΔG/G but doubles the noise (σ = 2 T_sys/sqrt(Bτ)). A correlating interferometer has no DC output, so gain fluctuations do not act on the whole system temperature, and uncorrelated noise averages to zero. For the panel this means one of two things. Either use beam/null switching with the true-time-delay states and keep a night-time Sun-absent offset table, because coupled receiver noise and correlated ground emission dominate the 25 mm-pitch correlations. Or correlate against a separate antenna metres away.

At 2695 MHz, 12 panel elements correlated with a 13 dBi grid on an external port 1-2 m away: Sun visibility 0.96-0.99, correlation 0.015, SNR about 70 per second, fringe period 25 or 13 min (east-west baseline, at transit). Ground and sky correlation drops below 0.2 %, and flux precision is about 0.2 % per minute (statistics only). A whip in place of the grid still gives SNR about 18 per second. At 408 MHz, two whips 5-10 m apart give SNR about 130 per second with 17-34 min fringes. At 1420 MHz, 10-20 m starts to resolve the disk (visibility 0.74 and 0.21).
findings.source: sun_tables.txt E (estimate: uniform disk 1.05-1.3 times the optical diameter)

findings.topic: The Sun as a calibration source where rev B may not radiate
findings.claim: The Sun radiates across the whole band, including the FCC 15.205 restricted slices where rev B is forbidden to radiate (2.69-2.9 GHz and 3.6-5.15 GHz except 4.4-4.5 GHz). There, REDESIGN accepts 1-2° of extra direction-finding error. Each element's phase, decoded by toggling and correlated against a 12-element beam on the Sun, comes to 0.53-0.71° per minute at 2.8-4.8 GHz (20 MHz), or 0.5° in 1-2 min. Each point applies only along the Sun's daily track, and the night-time offset table is required.
findings.source: sun_tables.txt I (estimate, statistics only); REDESIGN.md sections 6 and 9

findings.topic: Radio sun compass for moving mounts
findings.claim: Measuring the Sun's direction gives the RF boresight's absolute heading without any magnetic sensor. Combined with gravity from the accelerometer, two vectors give full attitude (the TRIAD method). Estimated heading error: 0.11-0.23° for a 1-5 m baseline at 2695 MHz, or 0.5-1° from panel direction finding alone. A magnetometer's heading shifts 0.3-2.9° when storm-time field changes of 100-1000 nT cross a 20 µT horizontal field; HamSCI gives storm and substorm variations of tens to hundreds of nT.

NoRP has measured total flux and circular polarisation (Stokes I and V) at 1, 2, 3.75, 9.4, 17, 35 and 80 GHz, with 3.75 GHz running for over 70 years; 100 ms FITS data since 1994 are open via SDAS. Radio-loud flares usually exceed a few tens of percent circular polarisation. Whole-disk polarisation outside flares is mostly near 0 % even at high activity, because Hale's law makes the hemispheres cancel; it varies most at 3.75 GHz, since the gyroresonance spectrum peaks at 3-6 GHz. JVLA found gyroresonance was only 8 % of the full-Sun flux at 2.8 GHz.

findings.topic: What the single-polarisation panel can and cannot measure
findings.claim: The Sun's linear polarisation (Q, U) is effectively zero. The estimated coronal rotation measure is 2.6e4 to 2.6e8 rad/m², spreading the polarisation angle by 2.4 to 2.4e4 rad across 10 MHz at 2695 MHz. So one linear polarisation measures exactly I/2 and the V-pol panel has no flux bias. But a circular wave gives half power at every roll angle, so Stokes V is invisible however the panel is rotated. The rotation study's roll method recovers linear polarisation only.
findings.source: derivation in sun_tables.txt F3; https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fspas.2020.00057/full ; /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/rotation/tables.md section e

findings.claim: Two orthogonal linear feeds, cross-correlated, give V = 2 Im<XY*>, which reveals the sense of polarisation (x versus o mode, hence magnetic polarity and emission mechanism), plus sqrt(2) better sensitivity. With feed leakage d, an unpolarised Sun gives a false V of up to 2|d| I: 20 % at -20 dB and 6.3 % at -30 dB, falling to 2 % or 0.6 % once d is solved to 10 % by rolling the antenna against a linear source such as CAL-ANT. That is enough for flares (tens of %) but marginal for the quiet Sun (a few %). The cheapest route is a dual-polarised or ±45° slant antenna on two external ports; the fields study's V+H quadrant scheme would also work.

findings.topic: Bursts, receiver headroom and the planned GNSS
findings.claim: Even a 1e6 sfu burst gives only 2.0e4 K and -82.5 dBm in 20 MHz in the panel beam, far below where the channel amplifier compresses (about -20 dBm), so bursts raise the noise floor without overloading anything (18 dB in the beam, 21 dB on a 1.4 GHz whip). A 3 dBic GNSS patch with a 150 K system temperature loses 3.8 / 11.7 / 21.5 dB of C/N0 at 1e4 / 1e5 / 1e6 sfu, or 24.5 dB if the burst is fully right-hand circular. The December 2006 bursts of about 1e6 sfu disrupted GPS tracking (Cerruti et al. 2008, not fetched: HTTP 403); DRAO's F10.7 was 573.4 sfu at 20 UT on 2006-12-06.
findings.source: sun_tables.txt C and D (estimate) ; https://doi.org/10.1029/2007SW000375 ; DRAO fluxtable.txt

findings.topic: Ionospheric Faraday rotation (where Earth's magnetic field does act)
findings.claim: RM = 2.63e-13 · TEC · B_parallel (SI units). With B_parallel = 40 µT, a linear wave rotates 16-330° at 408 MHz, 1.3-27° at 1420 MHz and 0.4-7.5° at 2695 MHz for 5-100 TECU. ITU-R P.531 gives up to 108° at 1 GHz for about 30° elevation. This matters for linearly polarised satellites and radar echoes received by the V-pol panel at UHF, but not for the Sun.
findings.source: sun_tables.txt F2 ; https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-P.531/en (P.531-8 Table 3; text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ascalva--claude-spares-spare-iFcbz1/8b6bf486-3081-448c-8f46-b00ba3ebceb0/scratchpad/fields/itu.txt)

findings.topic: Do magnets mounted on the array help? (owner's question)
findings.claim: No. Air has no free electrons for a magnet to act on: even 1e4 cm^-3 gives f_p = 0.9 MHz and an index change of 5.5e-8 at 2.7 GHz. Copper's Hall angle μB is 4.4e-3 rad at 1 T. Vacuum birefringence is about 2.6e-24 at 1 T, against a Schwinger field of 4.41e9 T. The only RF devices magnets act through are biased ferrites (circulators, YIG filters), covered by other studies. The real effect is harm: a 25.4 mm N52 cube gives 3,780 µT at 10 cm, beyond the LIS3MDL's maximum range of ±16 G (1,600 µT), 473 µT at 20 cm, and 30 µT at 0.5 m, about Earth's 30-60 µT. Uncompensated, that is a heading error of up to about 37° at 0.5 m and 5° at 1 m.
findings.source: derivation in sun_tables.txt G2-G3 (Br 1.45 T is an estimate) ; https://www.adafruit.com/product/4479 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_magnetic_field

findings.topic: Hobby and citizen-science solar radio projects
findings.claim:
- e-CALLISTO: heterodyne spectrometer designed in 2006 by C. Monstein; 45-870 MHz, 62.5 kHz resolution, 200 channels per 0.25 s; data archived at FHNW; at least 150 stations watch the Sun around the clock.
- Radio JOVE (NASA, since 1999): new RJ 2.1 kits use an SDRplay RSP1B; observers log type III and type II bursts at HF.
- SuperSID (Stanford Solar Center, distributed by SARA): over 2,500 VLF monitors detect flares through sudden ionospheric disturbances.
- MIT Haystack SRT: several hundred built; student projects on the quiet Sun at 21 cm, solar interferometry, and millisecond bursts near 1400 MHz.
- HamSCI magnetometers: PNI RM3100 sensor, about 3 nT at 1 Hz.
array16 would extend amateur coverage to 0.87-6 GHz, where professional references include EOVSA (1-18 GHz, open spectrograms) and NoRP.

findings.claim: The USNO approximate solar coordinates (accurate to about 1 arcminute), with GNSS time and position, are enough for pointing. Check: on 2026-11-15 at 40°N, 0°E the peak elevation is 31.45° at 11:44 UTC, as expected. A panel on an equatorial mount, as DRAO's dishes are, keeps the Sun within ±60° for 7.6-8.0 h/day at any latitude, with a smallest scan angle equal to the declination (at most 23.4°, a loss of at most 0.56 dB). A panel facing the zenith gets 0 h at 40-50°N in winter. Re-steer every 15 / 10 / 6 min at 2.44 / 3.5 / 5.8 GHz to keep pointing loss under 1 %. Drift scans across the beam take 4.1 / 2.9 / 1.7 h and map the beam along the Sun's track. The panel's 26-62° beams meet DRAO's 1 % disk-taper rule automatically.

open_questions: Does preselector band B3 (HFCN-1200+ followed by LFCN-2750+) pass 2690-2700 MHz with low loss, and does any band pass 2750-2850 MHz (the F10.7 band)? Both Mini-Circuits datasheets returned HTTP 403, so the band edges are unchecked.

How large are the panel's coupled-receiver-noise and ground-correlation offsets at 2.69-2.7 GHz, and how fast do they drift with temperature? Edge VSWR is 3-4 there. These offsets set the floor for measuring the Sun with the panel alone, by switching or correlation, and for calibrating elements on the Sun. openEMS plus a night-time bench measurement would answer it.

What is the RF environment at the owner's site? Mobile broadband (n41) at 2496-2690 MHz and S-band radars at 2700-3000 MHz border the 2690-2700 MHz slot, and the panel's channel amplifier compresses near -20 dBm in-beam, so the robust gain state may be needed.
What are the owner's latitude and mount: fixed equatorial, zenith-facing, vertical, or moving? This sets the hours of Sun inside the ±60° scan cone; the owner's location was deliberately not assumed.

Should a dual-polarised or circular antenna go on two external ports, or should the panel get V+H quadrants, to measure Stokes V? If so, at which band: 1.4-2.7 GHz, where the activity component is relatively largest, or 3-6 GHz, where gyroresonance polarisation peaks?
Burst rate at solar maximum for one site: only 31 days of current (declining-phase) SWPC events were available; the NOAA yearly event archive over HTTPS timed out.
